agent.system_template:
You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

## 1. What does this tool do? *grex* is a library as well as a command-line utility that is meant to simplify the often complicated and tedious task of creating regular expressions. It does so by automatically generating a single regular expression from user-provided test cases. The resulting expression is guaranteed to match the test cases which it was generated from. This project has started as a Rust port of the JavaScript tool [*regexgen*](https://github.com/devongovett/regexgen) written by [Devon Govett](https://github.com/devongovett). Although a lot of further useful features could be added to it, its development was apparently ceased several years ago. The plan is now to add these new features to *grex* as Rust really shines when it comes to command-line tools. *grex* offers all features that *regexgen* provides, and more. The philosophy of this project is to generate the most specific regular expression possible by default which exactly matches the given input only and nothing else. With the use of command-line flags (in the CLI tool) or preprocessing methods (in the library), more generalized expressions can be created. The produced expressions are [Perl-compatible regular expressions](https://www.pcre.org) which are also compatible with the regular expression parser in Rust's [*regex* crate](https://crates.io/crates/regex). Other regular expression parsers or respective libraries from other programming languages have not been tested so far, but they ought to be mostly compatible as well. ## 2. Do I still need to learn to write regexes then? **Definitely, yes!** Using the standard settings, *grex* produces a regular expression that is guaranteed to match only the test cases given as input and nothing else. This has been verified by [property tests](https://github.com/pemistahl/grex/blob/main/tests/property_tests.rs). However, if the conversion to shorthand character classes such as `\w` is enabled, the resulting regex matches a much wider scope of test cases. Knowledge about the consequences of this conversion is essential for finding a correct regular expression f 12251 characters elided 3} 36 and \u{663} and (?:\u{d83d}\u{dca9}){2}\.$ $ grex -dgr ^I ♥{3} \d(\d and ){2}💩{2}\.$ $ grex -rs ^I\s♥{3}\s36\sand\s٣\sand\s💩{2}\.$ $ grex -rw ^\w ♥{3} \w(?:\w \w{3} ){2}💩{2}\.$ $ grex -Dr ^\D{6}36\D{5}٣\D{8}$ $ grex -rS ^\S \S(?:\S{2} ){2}\S{3} \S \S{3} \S{3}$ $ grex -rW ^I\W{5}36\Wand\W٣\Wand\W{4}$ $ grex -drsw ^\w\s♥{3}\s\d(?:\d\s\w{3}\s){2}💩{2}\.$ $ grex -drswW ^\w\s\W{3}\s\d(?:\d\s\w{3}\s){2}\W{3}$ ``` ## 6. How to build? In order to build the source code yourself, you need the [stable Rust toolchain](https://www.rust-lang.org/tools/install) installed on your machine so that [*cargo*](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/), the Rust package manager is available. **Please note**: Rust >= 1.70.0 is required to build the CLI. For the library part, Rust < 1.70.0 is sufficient. ```shell git clone https://github.com/pemistahl/grex.git cd grex cargo build ``` The source code is accompanied by an extensive test suite consisting of unit tests, integration tests and property tests. For running them, simply say: ```shell cargo test ``` Benchmarks measuring the performance of several settings can be run with: ```shell cargo bench ``` ## 7. Python extension module With the help of [PyO3](https://github.com/PyO3/pyo3) and [Maturin](https://github.com/PyO3/maturin), the library has been compiled to a Python extension module so that it can be used within any Python software as well. It is available in the [Python Package Index](https://pypi.org/project/grex) and can be installed with: ```shell pip install grex ``` To build the Python extension module yourself, create a virtual environment and install [Maturin](https://github.com/PyO3/maturin). ```shell python -m venv /path/to/virtual/environment source /path/to/virtual/environment/bin/activate pip install maturin maturin build ``` The Python library contains a single class named `RegExpBuilder` that can be imported like so: ```python from grex import RegExpBuilder ``` ## 8. WebAssembly support This library can be compiled to [WebAssembly (WASM)](https://webassembly.org) which allows to use *grex* in any JavaScript-based project, be it in the browser or in the back end running on [Node.js](https://nodejs.org). The philosophy of this project is to generate the most specific regular expression possible by default which exactly matches the given input only and nothing else. The produced expressions are [Perl-compatible regular expressions](https://www.pcre.org) which are also compatible with the regular expression parser in Rust's [*regex* crate](https://crates.io/crates/regex). Other regular expression parsers or respective libraries from other programming languages have not been tested so far, but they ought to be mostly compatible as well. ## 2.           Takes precedence over --non-spaces if both are set. Non-word characters which are also
          non-whitespace are converted to \W.

Escaping Options:
  -e, --escape
          Replaces all non-ASCII characters with unicode escape sequences

          Converts astral code points to surrogate pairs if --escape is set

Repetition Options:
  -r, --repetitions
          Detects repeated non-overlapping substrings and converts them to {min,max} quantifier
          notation

          Specifies the minimum quantity of substring repetitions to be converted if --repetitions
          is set
          
          [default: 1]

          Specifies the minimum length a repeated substring must have in order to be converted if
          --repetitions is set
          
          [default: 1]

          Replaces non-capturing groups with capturing ones

          Prints help information

          Prints version information

## 1. What does this tool do? *grex* is a library as well as a command-line utility that is meant to simplify the often complicated and tedious task of creating regular expressions. It does so by automatically generating a single regular expression from user-provided test cases. The resulting expression is guaranteed to match the test cases which it was generated from. This project has started as a Rust port of the JavaScript tool [*regexgen*](https://github.com/devongovett/regexgen) written by [Devon Govett](https://github.com/devongovett). Although a lot of further useful features could be added to it, its development was apparently ceased several years ago. The plan is now to add these new features to *grex* as Rust really shines when it comes to command-line tools. *grex* offers all features that *regexgen* provides, and more. The philosophy of this project is to generate the most specific regular expression possible by default which exactly matches the given input only and nothing else. With the use of command-line flags (in the CLI tool) or preprocessing methods (in the library), more generalized expressions can be created. The produced expressions are [Perl-compatible regular expressions](https://www.pcre.org) which are also compatible with the regular expression parser in Rust's [*regex* crate](https://crates.io/crates/regex). Other regular expression parsers or respective libraries from other programming languages have not been tested so far, but they ought to be mostly compatible as well. ## 2. Do I still need to learn to write regexes then? **Definitely, yes!** Using the standard settings, *grex* produces a regular expression that is guaranteed to match only the test cases given as input and nothing else. This has been verified by [property tests](https://github.com/pemistahl/grex/blob/main/tests/property_tests.rs). However, if the conversion to shorthand character classes such as `\w` is enabled, the resulting regex matches a much wider scope of test cases. # Interesting! For "aa","ab","ba" with -r: ^(?:ab|ba|a{2})$
# This means "aa" -> a{2}, "ab" and "ba" are not changed.
# The repetition detection is per-string, not across strings.

# For "abc","abcbc","abcbcbc" with -r:
# "abc" -> no repetition (a,b,c are all different)
# "abcbc" -> "a" + "bc" repeated 2 times -> a(?:bc){2}
# "abcbcbc" -> "a" + "bc" repeated 3 times -> a(?:bc){3}
# Combined: a(bc|(?:bc){2,3}) -> factored: a(?:bc|(?:bc){2,3})

# Let me trace through the algorithm for "abcbc" and "abcbcbc":
# "abcbc" tokens: [a,b,c,b,c]
# Find repetition: "bc" repeats 2 times at position 1 -> RepeatGroup([b,c], 2)
# New sequence: [a, RepeatGroup([b,c], 2)]
# "abcbcbc" tokens: [a,b,c,b,c,b,c]
# Find repetition: "bc" repeats 3 times at position 1 -> RepeatGroup([b,c], 3)
# New sequence: [a, RepeatGroup([b,c], 3)]
# "abc" tokens: [a,b,c]
# No repetition -> sequence stays [a,b,c]

# DFA from these three sequences:
# "abc" -> [a,b,c]: S0-a->S1-b->S2-c->S3(acc)
# "abcbc" -> [a,RG([b,c],2)]: S0-a->S4-RG([b,c],2)->S5(acc)
# "abcbcbc" -> [a,RG([b,c],3)]: S0-a->S6-RG([b,c],3)->S7(acc)
# 
# After minimization:
# S3,S5,S7 are all equivalent (accepting, no transitions) -> S_acc
# S2: transitions {c->S_acc}, NOT acc -> does S2 = S4? S4 has {RG([b,c],2)->S_acc}
#   S2 has {c->S_acc}, S4 has {RG([b,c],2)->S_acc} -> DIFFERENT transitions -> NOT equivalent
# S1: has {b->S2}. Is this equiv to S4 or S6?
#   S4 has {RG([b,c],2)->S_acc}, S6 has {RG([b,c],3)->S_acc}
#   None are equivalent to S1 ({b->S2})
#
# So the minimized DFA has many states... the RegexGroup tokens don't cause much merging.
# 
# The regex generation would give:
# suffix(S_acc) = ""
# suffix(S2) = "c"
# suffix(S5) = "(?:bc){2}"? No...
# 
# Wait - how is RepeatGroup represented as a regex string?
# RepeatGroup([b,c], 2) -> "(?:bc){2}"
# 
# suffix(S5) = "(?:bc){2}" (single transition RG([b,c],2)->S_acc, dest suffix="")
# suffix(S7) = "(?:bc){3}"
# suffix(S4) = "(?:bc){2}" + "" = "(?:bc){2}"
# suffix(S6) = "(?:bc){3}"
# suffix(S1) = "b" + suffix(S2) = "bc" + "" = "bc"
# 
# Hmm, S5 and S4 might be the same state? Let me re-examine.
# Actually S4 and S5 would merge because S4-RG([b,c],2)->S5 and S5 is accepting.
# After minimization, S5 would be absorbed into S4 which transitions directly to S_acc.
# Let me redo:
# 
# States: S0, S1, S2, S3(acc), S4, S5(acc), S6, S7(acc)
# 
# Equivalence classes initially:
# Accepting: {S3, S5, S7} -> but these have different transitions (empty)
# So S3 ~ S5 ~ S7 -> merged to S_acc
# 
# Non-accepting: {S0, S1, S2, S4, S6}
# Check S2: transitions {c -> S_acc}, not accepting
# Check S4: transitions {RG([b,c],2) -> S_acc}, not accepting
# Check S6: transitions {RG([b,c],3) -> S_acc}, not accepting
# S2, S4, S6 have different transition keys -> NOT equivalent
# 
# Check S1: transitions {b -> S2}, not accepting
# Check S0: transitions {a -> S1, a -> S4, a -> S6} = {a -> S1 ∪ {a -> S4} ∪ {a -> S6}}
#   Wait! All three sequences start with 'a', so S0 should have multiple 'a' transitions
#   pointing to different states... but a DFA can only have ONE transition per symbol!
#   
# OH WAIT. I misunderstood. The DFA is built from the TRIE, and in a trie,
# each node has at most one child per symbol. All three sequences start with 'a',
# so they all go to the SAME S1 state from S0 via 'a'.
# 
# But S1 can have multiple transitions for different symbols.
# From S1: after consuming 'a', the next symbol can be 'b' (for "abc") 
# or RG([b,c],2) (for "abcbc") or RG([b,c],3) (for "abcbcbc").
# 
# These are DIFFERENT tokens, so S1 has 3 transitions:
# S1 -b-> S2
# S1 -RG([b,c],2)-> S5(acc)  
# S1 -RG([b,c],3)-> S7(acc)
# 
# After merging S5 and S7 (both accepting, same structure) -> S_acc:
# S1 -b-> S2
# S1 -RG([b,c],2)-> S_acc
# S1 -RG([b,c],3)-> S_acc
# 
# So S1 has transitions: {b->S2, RG([b,c],2)->S_acc, RG([b,c],3)->S_acc}
# suffix(S_acc) = ""
# suffix(S2) = "c"
# suffix(S1): 
#   - b -> S2: "b" + "c" = "bc"
#   - RG([b,c],2) -> S_acc: "(?:bc){2}" + "" = "(?:bc){2}"
#   - RG([b,c],3) -> S_acc: "(?:bc){3}" + "" = "(?:bc){3}"
#   Combined: "bc|(?:bc){2}|(?:bc){3}"
#   Factored: "bc" is prefix of "(?:bc){2}" and "(?:bc){3}"? No, they have different forms.
#   Actually factor: "bc|(?:bc){2,3}" -> 
#   "bc" = (bc){1} and (?:bc){2} and (?:bc){3}
#   Combined: bc|(?:bc){2,3}
#   Factored: bc|(?:bc){2,3} -> (?:bc){1,3}? Or just (?:bc|(?:bc){2,3})?
# 
# The result is ^a(?:bc|(?:bc){2,3})$ which matches the grex output!
# So the factoring "bc|(?:bc){2}|(?:bc){3}" -> "bc|(?:bc){2,3}" is what I need.
# Specifically: (?:bc){2}|(?:bc){3} = (?:bc){2,3}

# This means I need to implement:
# - Merging of {n} and {m} quantifiers: (?:...){n}|(?:...){m} = (?:...){n,m}
# - This happens during the alternation building

echo "Need to implement RepeatGroup token and quantifier merging"

fn find_best_rep(seq: &[Token], min_count: usize, min_len: usize) -> Option<(usize, usize, usize)> {
    let n = seq.len();
    let mut best: Option<(usize, usize, usize, bool)> = None;
    
    for start in 0..n {
        let max_period = (n - start) / min_count;
        for period in min_len..=max_period {
            let pattern = &seq[start..start+period];
            let mut count = 0;
            let mut pos = start;
            while pos + period <= n && &seq[pos..pos+period] == pattern {
                count += 1;
                pos += period;
            }
            
            if count < min_count {
                continue;
            }
            
            let covered_end = start + period * count;
            let ends_at_end = covered_end == n;
            
            let better = match best {
                None => true,
                Some((b_start, b_period, b_count, b_ends)) => {
                    if ends_at_end && !*b_ends {
                        true
                    } else if !ends_at_end && *b_ends {
                        false
                    } else if count > *b_count {
                        true
                    } else if count < *b_count {
                        false
                    } else if start > *b_start {
                        true
                    } else if start < *b_start {
                        false
                    } else {
                        period > *b_period
                    }
                }
            };
            
            if better {
                best = Some((start, period, count, ends_at_end));
            }
        }
    }
    
    best.map(|(s, p, c, _)| (s, p, c))
}
</output>

                    let sub_alts: Vec<String> = token_pats.iter()
                        .map(|tp| concat_token_and_suffix(tp, dest_suffix, cfg))
                        .collect();
                    // Try to factor/merge these alternatives
                    let joined = sub_alts.join("|");
                    let factored = factor_regex(&joined);
                    alternatives.push(factored);
                }'''

content = content.replace(old, new)
with open('grex_impl/src/regex_gen.rs', 'w') as f:

print("Done")

pub fn has_top_level_alternation(s: &str) -> bool {
    let bytes = s.as_bytes();
    let mut depth = 0;
    let mut i = 0;
    while i < bytes.len() {
        match bytes[i] {
            b'\\' => i += 1,
            b'(' | b'[' => depth += 1,
            b')' | b']' => depth -= 1,
            b'|' if depth == 0 => return true,
            _ => {}
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    false

pub fn build_regexp(test_cases: &[String], cfg: &Config) -> String {
    // Filter empty strings
    let non_empty: Vec<&String> = test_cases.iter().filter(|s| !s.is_empty()).collect();
    
    if non_empty.is_empty() {
        return format_result("", cfg);
    }
    
    // Convert to token sequences
    let mut sequences: Vec<Vec<Token>> = non_empty.iter()
        .map(|s| string_to_tokens(s, cfg))
        .collect();
    
    // Deduplicate
    sequences.sort();
    sequences.dedup();
    
    // Apply repetition detection if needed
    if cfg.repetitions {
        sequences = sequences.into_iter()
            .map(|seq| process_repetitions(&seq, cfg.min_repetitions, cfg.min_substring_length))
            .collect();
    }
    
    // Build DFA
    let dfa = DFA::from_token_sequences(&sequences);
    
    // Minimize DFA
    let min_dfa = dfa.minimize();

    if non_empty.is_empty() {

input.command:
# The issue: "-" starts with '-' but doesn't start with "--", so it goes to the
# "_ if arg.starts_with('-') && !arg.starts_with("--")" branch.
# It then tries to parse "" (the empty string after '-') as short flags.
# This fails in the loop (no chars to iterate).
# Actually it should be fine since arg[1..] = "" so the loop doesn't execute.
# But then it falls through to the empty input check!
# 
# Actually the issue is different: "-" starts with '-', so it goes to the short flag parser.
# But it's treated as a flag with no flag char. Let me check:
# arg = "-", arg[1..] = "", so the loop `for ch in "".chars()` iterates nothing.
# So the "-" is parsed as a flag that does nothing, and input_args stays empty.
# 
# Then at the end: has_file=false, input_args is empty, config.input is empty.
# The validation fails: "no test cases provided".
# 
# The fix: explicitly handle "-" before the flag parsing:

cat > /tmp/fix_stdin.py << 'EOF'
with open('grex_impl/src/cli.rs', 'r') as f:
    content = f.read()

old = '''            _ if arg.starts_with('-') && !arg.starts_with("--") => {
                // Handle combined short flags like -dgr'''

new = '''            _ if arg == "-" => {
                // Single "-" means read from stdin
                input_args.push(arg.clone());
            }
            _ if arg.starts_with('-') && !arg.starts_with("--") => {
                // Handle combined short flags like -dgr'''

content = content.replace(old, new)
with open('grex_impl/src/cli.rs', 'w') as f:
    f.write(content)
print("Done")
EOF
python3 /tmp/fix_stdin.py
cd grex_impl && cargo build 2>&1 | grep "^error"

fn topological_sort(dfa: &DFA) -> Vec<usize> {
    let n = dfa.states.len();
    let mut visited = vec![false; n];
    let mut order = Vec::new();
    
    fn dfs(state: usize, dfa: &DFA, visited: &mut Vec<bool>, order: &mut Vec<usize>) {
        if visited[state] { return; }
        visited[state] = true;
        for &next in dfa.states[state].transitions.values() {
            if !visited[next] {
                dfs(next, dfa, visited, order);
            }
        }
        order.push(state);
    }
    
    dfs(dfa.initial, dfa, &mut visited, &mut order);
    order.reverse(); // now order[0] = initial
    order
}

pub fn factor_prefix(s: &str) -> String {
    let alts = split_alternations(s);
    if alts.len() <= 1 {
        return s.to_string();
    }
    
    // Find common prefix of all alternatives
    let prefix = common_prefix(&alts);
    if prefix.is_empty() {
        // Try suffix factoring
        return factor_suffix_of_alts(&alts);
    }
    
    // Remove prefix from each alternative
    let suffixes: Vec<String> = alts.iter()
        .map(|a| a[prefix.len()..].to_string())
        .collect();
    
    // Recursively process the suffixes
    let suffix_regex = if suffixes.iter().all(|s| s.is_empty()) {
        String::new()
    } else {
        let processed: Vec<String> = suffixes.iter()
            .filter(|s| !s.is_empty())
            .cloned()
            .collect();
        if processed.is_empty() {
            String::new()
        } else if processed.len() == 1 {
            processed.into_iter().next().unwrap()
        } else {
            // Some suffixes are empty (meaning prefix alone is acceptable)
            let has_empty = suffixes.iter().any(|s| s.is_empty());
            let non_empty: Vec<String> = suffixes.iter()
                .filter(|s| !s.is_empty())
                .cloned()
                .collect();
            
            let combined = if non_empty.len() == 1 {
                non_empty.into_iter().next().unwrap()
            } else {
                let factored = factor_suffix_of_alts(&non_empty);
                factored
            };
            
            if has_empty {
                make_optional_str(&combined)
            } else {
                make_group_if_needed(&combined)
            }
        }
    };
    
    format!("{}{}", prefix, suffix_regex)
}

# AH HA! The first call to combine_alternatives is for combining Y[S_acc] for two different paths!
# 
# First call: by_first="hell|fo" -> by_first_alts=["hell","fo"] -> by_last="hell|fo"
# This is combining "hell" and "fo" (two paths to some intermediate accepting state).
# 
# Second call: by_first="world|hell|foo" -> by_last="world|hell|foo" -> WRONG!
# 
# In the second call, the input is ["world","hell","foo"] which is the COMBINED set.
# 
# The issue: when combining intermediate paths in the forward computation,
# I'm combining Y[state] values which contain partial strings like "hell" and "fo".
# These get stored as "hell|fo" in Y[some_state].
# Then when I collect accepting_prefixes, I get partial strings, not full strings!
# 
# For "hello" "world" "foo":
# DFA states after minimization:
# Let's say: S0-h->S_h-e->S_he-l->S_hel-l->S_hell-o->S_acc
# S0-w->S_w-o->S_wo-r->S_wor-l->S_worl-d->S_acc
# S0-f->S_f-o->S_fo-o->S_acc
# After min: S_acc (all three end at accepting), but also sharing of states.
# 
# Actually: "hell" and "fo" as Y values means the combining is happening for the
# S_hell state (accepting?) or the S_fo state in the path to S_acc.
# 
# Actually "hell" + "o" = "hello" and "fo" + "o" = "foo".
# The intermediate state S_acc for 'o' is shared between the "hello" and "foo" paths!
# Y[S_prev_acc] = "hell" | "fo" (two paths leading to the state before the final 'o')
# Y[S_acc] = S_prev_acc's Y + "o" = ("hell"|"fo") + "o" = "hell|fo" + "o"
# 
# But "hell|fo" + "o" should be "(?:hell|fo)o"!!!
# The issue is in concat_prefix when the prefix has top-level alternation.

grep -n "fn concat_prefix" /workspace/grex_impl/src/regex_gen.rs

# Great improvement! Only 3 failures now. Let me analyze:
# 
# 1. "a" "b" "x" "de" -> ^(?:[abx]|de)$ vs ^(?:de|[abx])$
#    Both are correct, just different ordering.
#    The expected "de|[abx]" has "de" (longer string) first.
#    Mine has "[abx]|de" with char class first.
#    
#    In my combine_alternatives, I sort by length:
#    "[abx]"(5 chars regex) > "de"(2 chars regex) -> "[abx]" first.
#    But expected has "de"(matches 2-char strings) first.
#    
#    This is the CONTENT-LENGTH vs REGEX-LENGTH issue I noticed before.
#    
# 2. "-r" "b" "ba" "baa" "baaa" -> ^ba{1,3}?$ vs ^b(?:a{1,3})?$
#    "ba{1,3}?" is wrong: it means "ba{1,3}" optionally = (a{1,3})?
#    But the issue: "a{1,3}?" means "a{1,3}" is optional -> {1,3}? = 0 or 1 occurrence of a{1,3}.
#    The correct: b + (a{1,3})? = b(?:a{1,3})?
#    
#    Mine: "ba{1,3}?" -> this comes from the make_optional_str("a{1,3}").
#    "a{1,3}" has split_into_units = ["a{1,3}"] -> len=1 -> IS single unit -> "a{1,3}?".
#    Then concat_prefix("a{1,3}?", "b") = "ba{1,3}?" which is WRONG.
#    Should be "b(?:a{1,3})?".
#    
#    The issue: "a{1,3}" is treated as a "single unit" so its optional form is "a{1,3}?".
#    But "a{1,3}?" = a repeated 1 to 3 times, optionally = a repeated 0 to 3 times. That's a{0,3}.
#    Not what we want!
#    The correct optional form of "a{1,3}" should be "(?:a{1,3})?" or just adjust the quantifier.
#    
#    Actually: "a{1,3}?" in regex means "a" repeated 1-3 times, with the '?' making the
#    quantifier LAZY (non-greedy), not optional! This is a common mistake.
#    "a{1,3}?" = match 'a' 1-3 times but lazily.
#    What we want: "(a{1,3})?" = 0 or 1 occurrence of the pattern a{1,3}.
#    
#    Fix: is_single_regex_unit for "a{1,3}" should return false (since it's already quantified),
#    or make_optional should check if the string already has a quantifier and wrap with group.
#
# 3. "-g" "-i" "big" "BIGGER" -> (?i)^big(?:ger)?$ vs (?i)^big(ger)?$
#    The -g flag should use capturing groups instead of non-capturing.
#    Mine uses (?:ger)? instead of (ger)?.
#    The issue: make_optional in combine_alternatives doesn't use cfg for capturing groups.

# 
# The simplest fix: after generating the regex, do a post-process to replace

# The issue: "world" has 5 atoms while "(?:hell|fo)o" has 2 atoms.
# My sort puts more atoms (world=5) first. But expected puts less atoms (2) first.

# Let me reconsider the sort criteria.
# For "ccc|bb|a" -> ccc first (3 atoms > 2 > 1). This uses "more atoms first" ✓.
# For "(?:(?:hell|fo)o|world)" -> "(?:hell|fo)o" before "world"...
# "(?:hell|fo)o" has 2 atoms but matches 2 different strings (5 and 3 chars).
# "world" has 5 atoms and matches 1 string (5 chars).
# 
# The difference: "(?:hell|fo)o" is a GROUPED alternative that matches multiple strings.
# "world" is a literal string.
# 
# Maybe the criterion should be: grouped alternatives (those with "(?:") come first?
# OR: sort by the MAXIMUM possible match length (longer = first)?
# "(?:hell|fo)o" max = 5 chars ("hello"), "world" = 5 chars. EQUAL.
# Then... number of distinct strings? "(?:hell|fo)o" = 2 strings, "world" = 1. More = first?
# 
# This is getting very complicated. Let me try a different approach:
# Instead of sorting by atoms, sort by REGEX LENGTH (longer regex string = first).
# "(?:(?:hell|fo)o|world)" vs "(?:world|(?:hell|fo)o)" - the (?:hell|fo)o is longer regex.

# 
# Hmm. OK let me think differently.
# 
# The sort should be: what comes from DEEPER in the DFA first.
# "(?:hell|fo)o" comes from the state that has the shared 'o' transition (shared between hello and foo paths).
# "world" comes from a single 5-step path.
# 
# In terms of Y[state] depth: "(?:hell|fo)o" is a COMBINED path that's been factored.
# The original paths were "hello"(5 chars) and "foo"(3 chars).
# "world" is 5 chars.
# 
# Maybe: sort by max path depth? Max("hello","foo") = 5, "world" = 5. Tie!
#

#

# Hmm. Let me just try: sort by whether the alternative IS a GROUP or not.
# "(?:hell|fo)o" starts with "(?:" -> it's a group expression -> complex.
# "world" doesn't start with "(" -> it's a literal sequence.
# Put GROUP expressions before LITERAL sequences? 
# "(?:hell|fo)o" is group+literal, "world" is all-literal.
# Group expressions first -> "(?:hell|fo)o" before "world" ✓?
# 
# But what about "ccc|bb|a"? These are all literals, sorted by length.

cd /workspace

# Run all the key examples from the README:
echo "=== Testing against known expected outputs ==="

declare -A tests=(
    ["'hello' 'world'"]='^(?:hello|world)$'
    ["'a' 'b' 'c'"]='^[a-c]$'
    ["'abc' 'bc'"]='^a?bc$'
    ["'foo' 'bar' 'baz'"]='^(?:ba[rz]|foo)$'
    ["'a' 'b' 'bcd'"]='^(?:b(?:cd)?|a)$'
    ["'abc' 'abcd'"]='^abcd?$'
    ["'a' 'aa' 'aaa'"]='^a(?:aa?)?$'
    ["'foo' 'foobar'"]='^foo(?:bar)?$'
    ["'-r' 'b' 'ba' 'baa' 'baaa'"]='^b(?:a{1,3})?$'
    ["'-r' 'aa' 'bcbc' 'defdefdef'"]='^(?:a{2}|(?:bc){2}|(?:def){3})$'
    ["'-i' 'big' 'BIGGER'"]='^(?i)big(?:ger)?$'
)

pass=0; fail=0
for args in "${!tests[@]}"; do
    expected="${tests[$args]}"
    # Remove the leading ^ from expected since it's in the regex itself
    mine=$(eval "./executable $args" 2>&1)
    if [ "$mine" = "${expected#^}" ] || [ "$mine" = "$expected" ]; then
        pass=$((pass+1))
    else
        # Try without ^ in expected comparison
        exp_clean="${expected}"
        if [ "$mine" = "$exp_clean" ]; then
            pass=$((pass+1))
        else
            fail=$((fail+1))
            echo "FAIL: $args -> '$mine' != '$expected'"
        fi
    fi
done
echo "Passed: $pass, Failed: $fail"

readme_tests["'a' 'b' 'c'"]="^[a-c]$"
readme_tests["'abc' 'bc'"]="^a?bc$"
readme_tests["'a' 'b' 'bc'"]="^(?:bc?|a)$"
readme_tests["'foo' 'foobar'"]="^foo(?:bar)?$"
readme_tests["'foo' 'bar' 'baz'"]="^(?:ba[rz]|foo)$"
readme_tests["'abc' 'abcd'"]="^abcd?$"
readme_tests["'a' 'aa' 'aaa'"]="^a(?:aa?)?$"
readme_tests["'-r' 'aa' 'bcbc' 'defdefdef'"]="^(?:a{2}|(?:bc){2}|(?:def){3})$"

# The problem: when we do `cd "$(dirname "$0")/grex_impl"`, 
# the $(dirname "$0") is evaluated AFTER the cd, so it returns the NEW working directory path.
# Actually $(dirname "$0") gets the directory of the script at the time of script execution.
# 
# The issue: after `cd .../grex_impl`, the relative `$(dirname "$0")/executable` 
# would be `.../grex_impl/../executable` which is... wait, let me trace:
# 
# If script is at /workspace/compile.sh:
# $(dirname "$0") = /workspace (absolute, since we gave absolute path? No...)
# 
# Actually, if run as ./compile.sh from /workspace:
# $0 = ./compile.sh
# dirname "$0" = "."
# "$(dirname "$0")/grex_impl" = "./grex_impl"
# After `cd ./grex_impl`, pwd = /workspace/grex_impl
# "$(dirname "$0")/executable" = "./executable" which is /workspace/grex_impl/executable!!
# 
# The fix: save the workspace dir before cd-ing:

cat > /workspace/compile.sh << 'COMPILEEOF'
#!/bin/bash
set -e

WORKSPACE_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"

# Check if Rust/Cargo is available
if ! command -v cargo &> /dev/null; then
    echo "cargo not found, installing Rust toolchain..."
    curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh -s -- -y
    source "$HOME/.cargo/env"
fi

echo "Building grex..."
cd "$WORKSPACE_DIR/grex_impl"
cargo build --release 2>&1

# Copy the binary to the workspace root
cp target/release/grex "$WORKSPACE_DIR/executable"
echo "Build complete: $WORKSPACE_DIR/executable"
COMPILEEOF

chmod +x /workspace/compile.sh
